html:
Rings of carved laterite pillars over burial grounds, set up along the Gambia River from about the 3rd century BCE to the 16th century CE. Wassu and Kerbatch in the Gambia and Sine Ngayene and Wanar in Senegal are the best known.

There are more than a thousand circles in a band about 350 km long, the densest group of such monuments anywhere. They show settled farming societies who could quarry and shape stone with iron tools long before written records. UNESCO listed them as a World Heritage Site in 2006. Who built them is still debated; they are older than the Mali Empire that later ruled the valley.
